newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FORECAST-HEINEKEN H1 NET SEEN BUOYED BY US EXPORTS.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-HEINEKEN H1 NET SEEN BUOYED BY US EXPORTS.

text.p: First half profits at Europe's biggest brewer Heineken NV are seen rising by over 10 percent, boosted by strong exports, particularly to a U.S. market thirsty for premium lager, analysts said on Tuesday.
They expect the brewer to post first half 1996 net profit of 308 to 322 million guilders, with the consensus at 316 million, versus 280 million in the year ago period.
"The main profits are coming from strong growth in exports, especially to the U.S.," said ING Barings analyst Gerard Rijk.
But analysts cautioned that poor summer weather and the saturated beer market in western Europe would dog sales in that region in the first half with a hangover into the second half.

"In Europe underlying sales are likely to have come under presure compared to last year...when it did so well," MeesPierson analyst Darrell Duthie said. "The question is how much the U.S market will compensate for weak European volumes."
It was this concern over second-half performance that jolted the share price 7.30 guilders lower on Tuesday to 362.90.
"In Europe we've seen bad summer weather...Now Heineken will know sales in July and August, it will likely anticipate slower (sales) growth in the second half," said Rijk.
Theodoor Gilissen analyst Dirk Erdman agreed the group's forecast for the remainder of 1996 would be followed closely.

Duthie said February's acquisitions of the Fischer Group in France and Italy's Birra Moretti SpA, would boost headline sales in the first half. But they would have limited impact on profits since they had lower margins than other Heineken units.
Analysts didn't expect any restructuring charges from the acquisitions to find their way to the first half balance sheet.
Analysts were split on the impact of currencies, in particular the dollar, on first half profits.
Rijk said there would be no negative effect from currencies, but Duthie was more cautious.

"My only hesitation (on currency affects) is Heineken's rolling hedging policy," said Duthie. "Exactly what rate they hedged last year's operating profit at is not clear so whether there will be a positive exchange rate affect is unsure."
Analysts agreed Heineken's withdrawl from Burma in July under mounting public pressure would have no bottom line affect.
"They are likely to have got out of Burma at book price, so there will be no affect at all," Duthie said.
As to emerging markets, analysts said ongoing investment there meant they would contribute little to overall net profit.
"Heineken has to invest a lot in emerging markets so I don't think they will have earned much there overall," said Erdman.
Heineken has a firm foothold in Far East markets through its Asia Pacific Breweries, 50/50 joint venture with Singapore-based Fraser and Neave Ltd.
